about: An original game inspired by The Wire (HBO, 2002-2008). Not affiliated with HBO or the show's creators. Every character, street, store, line of dialogue and phone number in it is invented.
Planned by Anthropic claude-opus-5-5 (reasoning effort max). Built by Anthropic claude-opus-5-5 (reasoning effort xhigh) in Claude Code: design, code, writing, music, sound and voices.
Engine: my-3D2dge v0.85.1 by Michael Crosato (MIT). Multiplayer: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, client 1.4.0.
No art, audio or font files: every picture, song, sound effect and gibberish voice is generated by code at run time. No third-party asset-store entries are used.
Penn Row is a fictional West Baltimore neighbourhood, October 2004. Real places stay generic: Central Booking, the courthouse, the Western District.
roll: Cornelius Felton, who called it in

sourceInformation.genre: Stealth investigation / crime drama, with a corner-management sim (playing the lieutenant) and an asymmetric hidden-identity versus mode (cops vs corner)
sourceInformation.perspective: Isometric 2.5D (pixel-art 3D skeletons on a tile world, camera turns in 90-degree steps); brawler-view interiors for the box, the wire room and chambers; HTML case-file screens over the game
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.1 full engine (canvas 2D renderer, iso view, E.Shell HTML HUD, standard pause/settings/controls/save slots); AI Hub session client 1.4.0 (shared-world); vanilla JavaScript (ES2020) in one IIFE; Web Audio; bundled to one HTML file by a Node 24 build script; no other libraries, no runtime network
sourceInformation.artDirection: Engine-native retro-modern pixel art (PS1-era 2D look) pushed toward grit: rowhouses, Formstone and boarded vacants as facades, sodium streetlight and rain at night, phone wires overhead with sneakers on them, shapes-as-data for cars, payphones and street furniture
sourceInformation.animation: Engine-native procedural Humanoid rigs (walk, run, crouch, built-in poses) plus the game's own poses by post-processing joints with E.ik3 (sit, lean, phone, camera, smoke, count money, cuffed, hands up, reach, gun); tweens, timers and scripted sequences
sourceInformation.audio: Code-written chip music (theme, field, corner, wire, chase, montage, versus and a gospel loop) on the engine's music clock with layers that rise with suspicion, synthesized effects (shutter, pager, DTMF, sirens, cuffs, reels), Web Audio ambience beds, and an Animalese-style formant gibberish voice per character, synced letter by letter, with a telephone filter on the wire
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, shared-world, 1-4 players: host-authoritative versus round (10 Hz snapshots under 1,100 bytes, client-moved own character with a host speed check, validated actions, leave-to-bot, time-up, server host, hidden-tab stepping). Local versus with bots or two players in split screen. No other network use
sourceInformation.testing: Lightweight testing as TASK.md allows (FPS and optimization out of scope), all run on the final build. (1) A gameplay chain (tests/complete.mjs): one Node run on the engine's fixed-step clock plays The Case from New Case to the credits with state flowing mission to mission, finishing every one of the 48 beats through its own mechanics (the camera's read and shutter, the stick held toward a goal for the chase and the rescue, Dana walking a tail along Tee's own trail with no suspicion edits, the box's four answers, the wire's minimize and log, the cipher wheel, the Board's pins, the affidavit's picker, Tee's orders, pager and dialer for all five nights), then plays Path B from the same save to the credits; nights counted $2,590 / $1,570 / $1,810 / $1,930 against the plan's $1,500-2,000 targets. (2) Real-input browser sessions (Playwright for Python, Chromium) where every action is a key or mouse event: tests/play.py (title, Settings, attract and its exit, About, New Case, the whole cold open, the card, the Annex briefing, the car ride, a photo with right mouse held and a left click) and tests/play2.py (the chase on WASD + Shift with E to tackle and cuff; Corey's box on keys 1-4; both wires on T / Enter / I with a page decoded from the PAGER panel on the Q/E wheel; the paperwork, with the code card at the evidence cage and the affidavit at the desk on the arrow keys and Enter; the Board, walked to and pinned on the arrow keys and Enter; Tee's night, with orders on the Q wheel and the pager on Tab; a bots versus round on WASD with a photo), loading the chain's saves where a beat needs earlier evidence. (3) A headless suite (boot and data validation, cipher tables, perception targets, the corner ledger, box rules, affidavit scoring, Board ties, all beats entered, both story paths walked, the Brass shutdown, Tee's night to the 2 AM count, the camera after a night, a pursuit bot catching Corey on the plan's chase values, bots-only versus rounds, the attract reel). (4) Chromium and WebKit browser checks (fake DualSense: PlayStation glyphs, the Xbox switch, both stick inversions; mouse hover focus and click; iPhone touch-only notice and Settings; attract on touch). (5) The AI Hub harness's four runs (2 players; 4 at 150 ms latency, 50 ms jitter, 5% loss; host leave; server host), all PASS. (6) The plan's versus balance test, 20 bots-only 5-minute rounds: corner 11, detail 8, draw 1, after tuning the quota and evidence points as the plan instructs. (7) viewport-matrix: 24 phone, foldable, tablet and desktop shots in Chromium, WebKit and Firefox, all clean, and about 25 screenshots looked at by eye. Headless Chromium on this shared machine crashed pages now and then (a compositor fault in the browser, also logged before this session); those runs were repeated, and the wire room passed in Firefox as well.
sourceInformation.research: Read the my-3D2dge handoff docs (README, API.md, the relevant parts of API-INDEX.md and AI_GUIDE.md, docs/ASSETS.md, the stealth kit and template game) and the AI Hub protocol README and harness; knowledge of the series from memory; no other web research
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown
sourceInformation.usage: Session time about 6 hours by the system clock (12:58 to about 19:00 on 2026-11-03); API cost and token counts unknown

testingFeedback: About 40 real issues in the game, plus 14 mistakes in my own tests. The data check flagged a voice and a crowd point inside a wall; the build's parse caught two syntax errors, and later a comment that swallowed the versus round's own counters; the AI Hub harness caught AIHub.ready() never being called; browser checks caught touch-only detection failing in WebKit and the idle timer running on game time; longer headless runs caught Tee's nights never reaching the 2 AM count, a count screen that never ended the night, a parked car firing its arrival every frame (a thousand knockers), a corner that stalled for good after its first shutdown, a pursuit that made Dana walk, an affidavit picker that hid the strongest evidence, and versus balance bugs (a per-detective ACT cap, a stash bonus paid again at every spot, bot shutdowns that never reopened or never stopped, a stash spot the runner could never reach); playing the whole story through its mechanics caught Tee's night switching Dana's camera off for good (no photo could be taken after the first night) and the truck's plate photo that could never come into focus; the real-input sessions caught Tab opening Dana's notebook instead of Tee's pager, the Board pulling Tee off Lieutenant when tied to his phone, the wire room's pages and the box's Continue being unreachable on a controller, and the mouse photo bug (browsers send chorded buttons as pointermove); screenshots caught stacked screens bleeding through, missing font glyphs, rowhouses hiding the player, washed-out dusk, the HUD prompt over dialogue, a leaked function in an objective line, overflowing signs, chambers framed off-centre and the DEMO badge under the corner button.

Thirteen. AIHub.ready() was scheduled just before a scene change, so every online round would have been voided; Tee's nights could not reach their count, and once they did, the count screen never ended the night; after Tee's first night Dana's camera never took another photo; the truck plate photo could never focus; a parked car fired its arrival every frame; the corner stalled for good after its first shutdown; a comment swallowed the versus round's counters; on a controller the box's Continue could not be pressed, so every interview was a dead end; mouse players could not take photos; the boot-time data report halted the boot screen; the touch-only notice did not appear on the iPhone profile; and in versus the runner could never reach one stash spot.

Playing the whole story through its mechanics in one chain (tests/complete.mjs), with the real-input sessions close behind. The chain found the deadlocks and the dead camera that every structural test had passed, because it needs each mission to actually finish; the real-input sessions found the controller dead ends (the box's Continue, the wire's pages, Tee's pager, the Board's phone ties) that no direct function call can see. The AI Hub harness was the most valuable single run: it found the ready() bug that would have broken every session.

The structural walkers: 'all 48 beats enter and run' and 'the Director walks the story on both paths' passed while the interludes deadlocked and the camera was dead after the first night, because they skip the gameplay. The first perception test was also weak: it placed Dana inside a wall and measured its own mistakes.
engineFeedback: How much comes free and works with every device: pause menu, settings with my own game settings beside them, rebinding, save slots, E.Shell's HUD and toasts, input.label giving PlayStation or Xbox glyphs, and the exact fixed-step headless mode that made a 48-beat smoke test and a perception tuning test cheap. Procedural Humanoids and shapes-as-data meant a whole cast and a street full of cars and payphones with no art files.

Yes, a few times: game.after timers are cleared on a scene change (that cost the hub ready() bug); a boot step that calls game.fail halts the boot screen; cam.offset's sign puts the focus right of centre for positive x; rotateView is relative; the default cutaway only cuts the one wall row next to open floor, which is not enough for deep rowhouse blocks; the 5x7 font has no middle dot, ellipsis or em dash; E.Suspicion rises linearly with exposure, so simple presence eventually makes you unless you subtract a baseline.

A controller-first DOM screen kit (spatial focus, hover focus, legends that follow the last device, stacked screens that cooperate with the engine's pause) for the Board, notebook, cipher, box, affidavit and wire room. Close behind: the Animalese formant voice with a telephone filter, and the CornerSim that runs the same corner for story, Tee's nights, versus and attract.

Framing a dense isometric city: tall rowhouse blocks hide the player, so I replaced the cutaway rule with a focus-aware cone. Second, sharing input between the engine's pause menu and my own DOM screens (Escape both pauses and backs out), which needed the scene's pausable flag held while a screen is open.
The cutaway: make it focus-aware (lower every wall between the camera and the followed body, in a cone) instead of only the row next to open floor.

A keep option on game.after and game.every like tweens and scripts have, and a documented per-step hook that runs before every scene's update; together they would have removed a whole class of scene-change bugs.
promptFeedback: It is precise where precision matters: the exact file name, the exit-interview shape, and concrete 10-foot UX rules (PlayStation glyphs with an Xbox setting, both stick inversions for the known pad bug, prompts that follow the last device, a touch-only notice, a 10-second attract mode). Those are testable, so I could prove them.

The plan's file stem (max, 105319) differs from TASK.md's (xhigh, 125815); TASK.md wins, but it is easy to miss. 'Keep testing lightweight' sits beside a plan with a long test list. The Usage field asks for cost and tokens, which a run cannot see from inside.

Scope, and proving it: five story episodes with interludes, a versus mode with real netcode, an attract reel and a controller-first UI, all without stubs. The hard part was not writing each system but showing that the whole story finishes through play on the plan's own numbers, and that every screen works from a controller and not only from a mouse.

A real person playing the whole story start to finish with a DualSense on a TV, and once on a real iPhone in Safari. The automated chain and the real-input sessions prove that every mission finishes and every screen answers the controls; only a human proves the pacing and the 10-foot readability over an hour.

aiHub.name: WIRETAP
aiHub.description: Work both sides of a West Baltimore corner in 2004: build a wiretap case one photo, page and phone call at a time, then run the corner the case is built on. Includes a 1-4 player cops-versus-corner hidden-identity mode.
aiHub.controls: Stick/WASD move · L2/right mouse watch · R2/left mouse photo · ✕/E interact · △/Q partner and orders · Create/Tab notebook
